Market impact will hinge on what traders had already positioned for confrontation—distinguishing between a meaningful reprieve and modest repricing across energy stocks and equities.

lvmh-fenty-beauty-exit.headline: LVMH in exit talks over Fenty Beauty stake as digital-luxury valuations cool
lvmh-fenty-beauty-exit.body_md:
LVMH is exploring the sale of its 50 percent stake in Fenty Beauty — the cosmetics brand it co-founded with Rihanna in 2017 — in a move that crystallises a broader repricing of high-profile, founder-led beauty assets across the luxury sector.

Jay-Z's investment platform MarcyPen Capital Partners is reportedly the frontrunner to acquire the stake. The firm was formed in 2024 when Marcy Venture Partners merged with Pendulum Opportunities and now manages roughly $1.1 billion in assets. A deal would leave Rihanna's 50 percent stake intact, keeping ownership of the brand firmly within Black creative entrepreneurship even as the corporate architecture shifts.

JPMorgan has valued LVMH's half of the business at between €1.5 billion and €2.5 billion. Investment bank Evercore has been engaged to run the process. No official statement has come from either LVMH or Rihanna's camp — the silence customary at this stage, and given the headline sensitivity of the asset, probably deliberate.

## A portfolio reset with a long list

The Fenty exit does not stand alone. LVMH is in the middle of what analysts have called its most significant portfolio restructuring in nearly four decades. Marc Jacobs was sold for $850 million to a joint venture between WHP and G-III. The group is also reported to be weighing exits from Make Up For Ever and Fresh, the US brand founded in 1991. LVMH stock — down roughly 23 percent year-to-date through mid-June — underscores the pressure on management to defend returns.

The deeper logic may be Armani. Following Giorgio Armani's death in September 2025, LVMH emerged alongside L'Oréal and EssilorLuxottica as a named preferred buyer for a stake in the Italian house, with a full transfer expected to unfold over three to five years at a potential valuation approaching €10 billion. A deal at that scale demands balance-sheet headroom, and trimming the beauty division is one way to find it.

Fenty Beauty itself is not a distressed asset. The brand generated an estimated $450 million in net sales in 2024, having famously crossed $100 million in its first 40 days on shelves back in September 2017. The question LVMH is implicitly answering is not whether Fenty is valuable — it plainly is — but whether a minority stake in a founder-controlled brand fits the portfolio the group wants to own as it reaches for larger, more structurally complex acquisitions.

The timing also speaks to a broader moment in celebrity beauty. Rhode, Hailey Bieber's skincare line, sold to e.l.f. Beauty for $1 billion earlier this year; Rare Beauty has reportedly fielded interest from acquirers. The initial wave of valuation euphoria that greeted direct-to-consumer beauty launches is giving way to harder questions about margin structure, brand longevity beyond the founder's cultural moment, and whether the strategic uplift of celebrity association translates to durable returns.

What to watch: whether MarcyPen moves from reported frontrunner to confirmed buyer, and how LVMH characterises the exit publicly — as portfolio discipline or as a vote of confidence in a brand mature enough to stand without a luxury conglomerate's balance sheet behind it. The framing will say something about what the group believes it got out of nine years as Rihanna's co-founder.

boeing-services-backlog-record.headline: Boeing services unit hits record $33bn backlog as recurring revenue rebuilds
boeing-services-backlog-record.body_md:
Boeing's aftermarket division reported a record $33 billion backlog at the end of the first quarter, its highest ever, as the company continues pushing its services unit toward the front of its recovery story.

> **Boeing Global Services booked $8 billion in new orders in Q1 2026, pushing its backlog to a record $33 billion — a book-to-bill ratio of 1.6x that signals demand running well ahead of current output.**

Revenue for the segment reached $5.4 billion in Q1 2026, a 6% rise on the prior-year period. Strip out the impact of Boeing's recently divested Digital Aviation Solutions unit, and the organic growth rate comes closer to 13%. Operating earnings were $971 million at an 18.1% margin — down modestly from 18.6% a year earlier, a decline the company attributes directly to that divestiture rather than underlying deterioration.

For a company that spent much of 2024 working through a crippling machinists' strike and serial certification delays, a services business generating near-20% operating margins is a meaningful counterweight. Boeing's commercial airplane and defense segments have long dragged on the blended margin profile; Global Services does not.

![Singapore Airlines Boeing 777-300ER, one of the aircraft types covered under the new landing gear exchange programme](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c6/Boeing_777-300ER_Singapore_Airlines.JPG)

## Contracts and what they signal

The quarter's headline win — and a useful illustration of what the backlog actually represents — was the largest Landing Gear Exchange Program agreement in Boeing's history, signed with Singapore Airlines Group at February's Singapore Airshow. The deal covers more than 75 aircraft across Singapore Airlines' and low-cost subsidiary Scoot's combined 737 MAX and 787 fleets. Under exchange-program structures, Boeing supplies overhauled gear from managed inventory rather than waiting for each airline to pull its own units offline; the economics favor the carrier on downtime and favor Boeing on parts throughput and long-term contract lock-in.

William Ampofo, Boeing Global Services' senior vice president for parts and supply chain, described the logic simply: "This agreement helps deliver parts faster and closer to operations — reducing downtime and supporting consistent, reliable service."

The division also received initial FAA and EASA qualification for 777-9 flight-simulator training devices during the quarter, extending its footprint into the training segment as the widebody's entry into service draws nearer.

## One quarter, not a trend line

The structural argument for services is straightforward: once an aircraft enters a customer's fleet, the manufacturer has a captive addressable market for maintenance, parts, training, and digital tools across a 25-30 year operational life. Airbus and RTX have made exactly this pivot, and their aftermarket businesses now carry meaningfully richer valuation multiples than the hardware side.

Boeing trades at roughly 1.6 times forward sales, against an industry average closer to 2.5 times. That discount reflects the company's broader baggage — unresolved certification timelines, a debt load that remains uncomfortable, and the ongoing question of whether production-rate recoveries on the 737 and 787 will hold. A single strong quarter in services does not resolve any of those overhangs.

CEO Kelly Ortberg, in the Q1 earnings release, framed the results as momentum rather than arrival: "We're building on our momentum with a strong start to the year and growing record-breaking backlog across our business."

What closes the valuation gap, if anything does, is sustained sequential growth in services revenue coupled with proof that the commercial programs can deliver at scale. The Q2 earnings call — due in late July — will be the next substantive read on whether the $33 billion backlog is translating into the cash flow traders need to see before re-rating the stock.

nvidia-etf-tax-trap-diversification.headline: Nvidia insiders with concentrated mega-gains explore ETF structures to sidestep capital-gains lock-in
nvidia-etf-tax-trap-diversification.body_md:
The math that made Nvidia insiders wealthy is the same math that now keeps them stuck. Shares accumulated in the early-to-mid 2010s have appreciated more than 400-fold on a split-adjusted basis over the past decade, and selling even a slice of those holdings triggers a federal capital gains bill — up to 20% on long-term gains, and as high as 37% on short-term — before state levies arrive. In California, where much of the company's workforce is concentrated, add another 13.3%. For holders sitting on positions worth tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, the resulting tax drag can easily consume a third of proceeds. The rational response, for many, has been to hold.

The aggregate scale of that paralysis is significant. Nvidia insider selling has exceeded $3.3 billion in recent years — a figure that represents only what holders chose to monetize at full cost. Jensen Huang, whose personal stake in the company represents the overwhelming share of his estimated net worth, holds tens of billions on paper. AllianceBernstein published research late last year describing the broader phenomenon as "unlocking the golden handcuffs" — a phrase that captures the structural bind: concentrated mega-gains are wealth, but not quite liquidity.

A growing corner of the financial industry is now pitching structured alternatives.

## Two tools, two very different strings attached

**Traditional exchange funds** are the longer-established route. Investors pool appreciated shares with others doing the same, receive a pro-rata interest in a diversified basket, and defer the capital gains event. The vehicle accepts concentrated single-stock positions — exactly the profile of a long-tenured Nvidia employee — and minimum investments typically start around $100,000. The cost: a mandatory seven-year holding period before withdrawing diversified shares without triggering recognition, and access limited to accredited investors and qualified purchasers.

The newer entrant is the **Section 351 ETF conversion**, which allows holders to contribute appreciated securities into a newly created ETF as a non-taxable event. The original cost basis carries over — taxes are deferred, not forgiven — but the structure offers immediate liquidity through ordinary exchange trading. Thirty-nine such ETFs launched in the United States between 2021 and 2025, seeding roughly $8.7 billion in investor assets. Tidal Financial Group, Cambria, and Alpha Architect are among the active facilitators.

The crucial limitation: the IRS imposes a strict diversification test. No single security can exceed 25% of contributed assets; the top five combined cannot exceed 50%. The rule was written precisely to prevent a concentrated position from being restructured tax-free without meaningful diversification — meaning a Nvidia insider whose portfolio is 90% a single stock cannot use a 351 conversion directly. Those who already hold a broader basket, and want to restructure it efficiently, have more options.

Donor-advised funds, hedged equity overlays, and direct indexing round out the menu, each with distinct eligibility walls and cost trade-offs ranging from roughly 0.40% to 1.50% annually across vehicle types.

The practical upshot is that most pure Nvidia insiders remain pointed toward the traditional exchange fund — accepting the seven-year lockup as the price of diversification. Whether demand for these instruments accelerates will depend in part on whether proposed changes to federal capital gains rates advance in the current Congress. Any upward revision from the current 20% ceiling would sharpen the incentive considerably, and make the seven-year handcuffs look like a bargain.

spacex-ipo-retail-chip-rotation.headline: SpaceX IPO draws retail cash from chip stocks ahead of Friday debut
spacex-ipo-retail-chip-rotation.body_md:
Three semiconductor names that led the AI-driven rally all spring got hit in the same window this week: Micron Technology fell 4.7% on Wednesday, Qualcomm shed 6.9%, and Broadcom dropped 5.1%. The proximate cause wasn't an earnings miss or a macro surprise. It was a rocket company.

SpaceX began trading on Nasdaq today under the ticker SPCX, priced at $135 a share — a fixed, take-it-or-leave-it figure set by Elon Musk rather than shaped through the conventional bookbuilding process. The offering raises $75 billion and implies a valuation of roughly $1.75 trillion, making it the largest IPO in stock market history. In the days before that debut, retail traders were liquidating positions in some of the most-owned names in their portfolios to get there.

## The Drawdown in Chip Land

![SpaceX Starship on the launch pad at Boca Chica](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3a/Starship_full_stack.jpg)

The data is unambiguous, if the interpretation is still contested. Vanda Research tracked non-professional traders selling individual stocks for three consecutive days through Wednesday — the first such streak since March 2020, when the pandemic triggered a different kind of forced liquidation. Monday alone generated what Vanda called the largest retail cash pull from single-name equities since November 2023.

"Evidence so far is that retail may be saving some dry powder for these upcoming IPOs," said Viraj Patel of Vanda Research. Greg Boutle of BNP Paribas was more pointed about the chip names specifically, describing Micron's drop as consistent with "selling flows in recent winners and levered products" being unwound to fund SpaceX participation.

Micron, Qualcomm, and Broadcom aren't random targets. They were the core holdings of the retail AI trade in the first half of 2026, their valuations built in part on the assumption that the semiconductor supercycle had further to run. Advanced Micro Devices and Super Micro Computer also showed weakness in the same window. The selling wasn't a market-wide flush; it was concentrated in the names retail had been building since January.

The concern, articulated by Douglas Beath at Wells Fargo, is about the residual effect: "Selling existing stocks, tech and non-tech, could lead to issues and volatility down the line through the rest of the year." He suggested the setup "could cause some indigestion," though he stopped short of predicting sustained declines. One structural backdrop amplifies the risk: U.S. household equity holdings now sit at 35% of total financial assets, an all-time high — meaning the marginal retail seller has more concentrated exposure to swing than at almost any point on record.

## What SpaceX Is Selling — And What It Isn't

The $75 billion SpaceX attracted in retail orders didn't arrive on blind faith. The company did something structurally unusual: reserving up to 30% of its IPO for individual investors, compared with a sector norm of 5 to 10%. Fidelity lowered its account minimum to $2,000 to widen participation. Schwab, Robinhood, SoFi, and Morgan Stanley's E-Trade joined as distribution platforms. Prediction markets on Polymarket gave a 65% probability that SPCX closes above $2 trillion in market cap on its first day.

The enthusiasm runs ahead of the fundamentals, at least by conventional metrics. The combined SpaceX-xAI entity — merged in February via an all-stock deal that valued the combination at $1.25 trillion — posted $18.67 billion in revenue in 2025 against a net loss of $4.94 billion. That loss marks a sharp reversal from 2024, when SpaceX on a standalone basis earned roughly $791 million. The culprit is xAI, which contributed $3.2 billion in revenue while burning approximately $14 billion in cash — consuming, by itself, more cash than the rest of SpaceX's operations generate. Starlink's economics remain strong, with adjusted EBITDA up 86% and subscriber counts doubled in 2025, but those numbers are now buried under a $14 billion AI infrastructure commitment.

Retail buyers are, in a real sense, exchanging proven earners in Micron and Broadcom for a bet on whether Starship, Starlink, and Grok can eventually justify a $1.75 trillion entry price. That isn't necessarily wrong — it is, however, a different risk profile from the one they held last Tuesday.

## The ETF Wave Arrives with a Warning

Brokerages aren't the only vehicles being positioned around SPCX. At least 25 ETFs tied to SpaceX have registered with the SEC ahead of the listing, with roughly a dozen structured as 2x leveraged products — both bull and bear versions. Defiance's SPCU, Tradr's SPCM and SPCG, and Leverage Shares' SPCH and SSPC are among those either launched or imminent.

Jared Blikre, markets editor at Yahoo Finance, flagged the standard risk in plain terms: "If you're looking for one of those 2X up or 2X bear products, you've got to be careful because these are meant for short-term investors." Daily resets, compounding decay on volatile underlyings, and the mechanics of synthetic leverage mean the ETFs can diverge substantially from the underlying stock's performance over any window longer than a single session. For retail buyers who held chipmakers for months and are now redirecting those proceeds, the leveraged wrapper introduces an entirely new layer of risk on top of an already concentrated IPO bet.

The broader question the week has raised is whether the rotation will persist past the IPO's first-day pop or reverse as enthusiasm normalizes. Chip stocks sold to fund SpaceX allocations don't automatically flow back if SPCX disappoints. And with OpenAI and Anthropic both expected to test public markets in the coming months, the same dynamic — retail liquidating existing tech positions to fund new listings — could repeat. The next catalyst to watch is SPCX's close today: if it finishes well above $135, expect the leveraged ETFs to open with significant inflows. If it struggles to hold its offer price, the chip stocks sold to get here may start looking like the better trade.

trump-cancels-iran-strikes-deal-hormuz.headline: Trump cancels Iran strikes as deal text is approved; Hormuz blockade to lift by weekend
trump-cancels-iran-strikes-deal-hormuz.body_md:
For three and a half months, the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow passage through which roughly one-fifth of the world's seaborne oil trade normally flows — has been effectively closed to commercial shipping. The disruption began on February 28 when United States and Israeli strikes killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei; Tehran responded by closing the strait and mining sea lanes, triggering what the International Energy Agency has called the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market. On Thursday evening, something shifted.

President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that he had cancelled scheduled strikes and bombings against Iran, citing discussions that had been "brought to the highest level of Iranian leadership and approved." Speaking to reporters at the White House, he went further: the Strait of Hormuz would reopen the moment a deal was signed, and that signing, he said, could come as soon as this weekend in Europe, with Vice President J.D. Vance in attendance. The naval blockade of Iranian ports, in place since April 13, would remain until the transaction was finalised.

## The text that landed

The mechanism behind Trump's announcement is a memorandum of understanding whose draft has been shuttled between Washington and Tehran for weeks by Qatari mediators. Al Arabiya reported Thursday that a Qatari delegation had returned from Tehran carrying Iran's approval of the final draft — the most concrete diplomatic movement in the negotiations to date.

The MOU's terms, as described by officials from mediating countries and confirmed in broad outline by multiple outlets, are structured around a 60-day window. The Strait of Hormuz would reopen immediately, without tolls, with traffic expected to recover to pre-war volumes within 30 days. Iran would receive temporary sanctions waivers allowing it to resume selling oil for the duration. In exchange, the ceasefire would extend through Lebanon, and nuclear negotiations would begin — covering Iran's stockpile of roughly 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent (well short of the 90 percent threshold for weapons-grade material) and a broader framework for its nuclear programme. Tehran would pledge not to pursue nuclear weapons; the harder question of enrichment itself would be deferred to a second, more detailed accord.

Iran's Fars News Agency — affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps — signalled that, given US acceptance of Iran's proposed text, approval from the Iranian side was likely. Iran's Foreign Ministry told state television a different story: reports of a finalised agreement were "merely speculation," and no final decision had been reached. That gap between the mediating countries' read and Tehran's public posture is recognisable as late-stage negotiating behaviour, but it is a real gap nonetheless.

## Parties not at the table

A discordant note came from Jerusalem. A senior Israeli official told Channel 12 that Israel had not been made aware of any finalised US–Iran agreement — appearing to contradict Trump's claim on Truth Social that parties including Israel, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Turkey, Pakistan, and others had all approved the deal in "both concept and great detail." Netanyahu's office subsequently framed their call with Trump more cautiously, describing a conversation about "the emerging memorandum of understanding with Iran regarding entry into negotiations" — language that stops well short of endorsement. Israel is not a signatory to any ceasefire and was not present at the negotiating table; its position matters because any resumption of Israeli strikes on Iran would almost certainly unravel whatever Washington and Tehran have agreed.

Trump simultaneously threatened to take Kharg Island — which handles roughly 90 percent of Iran's crude exports — if negotiations faltered, a warning that serves dual purpose: signalling resolve to Tehran and providing reassurance to Israel that Washington has not blinked.

## What the market had already priced in

Oil's reaction on Thursday reveals a market that had anticipated de-escalation — but not yet in full. Brent crude settled at $89.15, down 4.2 percent; WTI fell 3.9 percent to $86.51. European natural gas futures dropped as much as 4 percent alongside the moves. Those are meaningful single-session declines, but they follow a substantial retreat that had already been under way: Brent touched $138 per barrel on April 7, its highest level in four years, before sliding as ceasefire signals accumulated through May and June.

![Satellite view of the Strait of Hormuz and Musandam Peninsula. Roughly 600 tankers remain trapped inside the Persian Gulf; another 240 wait outside the strait.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/50/Strait_of_Hormuz_from_35%2C000_Feet.jpg)

The cumulative supply loss since Hormuz closed runs to some 880 million barrels. Around 600 tankers remain trapped inside the Persian Gulf; another 240 sit waiting on the ocean side. The strait's normal throughput is roughly 20 million barrels per day — the largest single maritime chokepoint in the global energy system. Saudi Aramco's chief executive, Amin Nasser, warned in May that oil market normalisation might not arrive until 2027 if the obstruction persisted.

Markets have been here before. Trump signalled on multiple occasions since March that a deal was days away, only for it to stall. Thursday's announcement carries more weight than those earlier statements — the Qatari delegation's return trip from Tehran is a concrete diplomatic movement, not a social media post — but the distance between "text agreed" and "deal signed" has repeatedly proven longer than anticipated. The 4 percent oil drop suggests traders believe Thursday was different; it also reflects roughly 35 percent of the price premium remaining, implying real scepticism about the weekend timeline.

## The weekend as deadline

The specific catalyst to watch is a formal signing. If Vance boards a plane to Europe and a ceremony takes place on schedule, the Hormuz reopening becomes contractually obligated — and oil markets, which have retreated from $138 to the upper eighties over ten weeks, would face a more nuanced set of questions: how much further supply normalisation is already assumed in spot prices, how fast the 600 trapped tankers can clear, and whether the nuclear talks that open in the 60-day window can hold.

Iran's Supreme Leadership — whoever formally holds that authority after Khamenei's death — must still provide written final approval. That sign-off is the variable Trump cannot deliver unilaterally, regardless of what the Qatari delegation carried back from Tehran. If it arrives before Sunday, the machinery for the largest oil-supply restoration in decades is in place. If it does not, the naval blockade holds, and the oil market's tentative $50-per-barrel retreat from its crisis peak faces its own test.

bitcoin-mallers-btc-prague.headline: Strike's Mallers calls Bitcoin below $63,000 'the only honest signal'
bitcoin-mallers-btc-prague.body_md:
Bitcoin has shed more than half its value since peaking above $126,000 in October 2025, and as of early June it was trading around $62,800—territory that has prompted the usual conference-circuit reassurances. At BTC Prague on Wednesday, Jack Mallers offered one of the more carefully constructed versions.

Mallers, who founded payments app Strike and also serves as co-founder and chief executive of Bitcoin treasury company Twenty One Capital (Nasdaq: XXI), told the Prague audience that Bitcoin trading below $63,000 is not a sentiment problem. It is, in his framing, "the only honest signal"—an unmanipulated readout of actual financial conditions in a system where other markets have been distorted beyond legibility.

"Bitcoin is the closest thing we have to the monetary reflection of truth," Mallers said. "Active 24/7 traded indicator of how the world is doing."

The move is rhetorical and deliberate. Bitcoin's critics read the 50%-from-peak decline as a risk-asset rout—no different from any other high-beta unwind. Mallers's construction inverts that: Bitcoin is behaving honestly *because* other markets are not.

His evidence for the disconnect: University of Michigan consumer sentiment has sunk below the floors of 2008, 2000, and the recessions of the early 1980s. The S&P 500, meanwhile, trades near all-time highs. The two data points, he argued, cannot both describe the same economy. One market is reporting fiction, and in his telling it is not the one that trades around the clock without a circuit breaker.

## The liquidity mechanism

The cause of the sell-off, Mallers argued, is not crypto-specific panic but a global cash scramble. Nations are simultaneously funding wars, artificial-intelligence buildouts, and expanding deficits. Individuals are behind on credit-card bills and rent. The result is forced liquidation across every asset class. "You sell what you can, not what you want," he said.

The market data from early June supports the broad picture, if not the specific interpretation. Bitcoin briefly touched $61,165 on June 4, triggering roughly $3 billion in leveraged-position liquidations in a single session. Spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $2.7 billion in outflows over the following week. Strategy—the corporate Bitcoin accumulator formerly known as MicroStrategy—completed its first Bitcoin sale since 2022, an event that attracted attention disproportionate to its size because the institutional-conviction narrative had been doing structural work.

The "honest signal" framing serves a specific constituency: Bitcoin holders who need a story that is neither panic nor denial, and who want the price weakness to confirm the thesis rather than threaten it. Mallers holds direct financial exposure through both Strike and Twenty One Capital, a circumstance that does not invalidate the argument but does clarify the incentive structure around it.

For traders, the speech offers softly bullish sentiment from a connected advocate—no new data on fundamentals, no strategy shift, no institutional catalyst. The more actionable indicators to watch are the Federal Reserve's next rate signal—May CPI came in at 4.2% against a 2% target—and whether Bitcoin ETF flows reverse as geopolitical risk fades following reports that a deal to lift the Strait of Hormuz blockade is expected to be finalized by the weekend.

trump-pacific-fishing-protection-reverse.headline: Trump opens federally protected Pacific Ocean zones to commercial fishing
trump-pacific-fishing-protection-reverse.body_md:
A presidential proclamation signed at the White House on Thursday removes commercial fishing restrictions from roughly half a million square miles of protected Pacific Ocean waters, rolling back conservation measures that have been in place across three marine national monuments for as long as two decades.

The proclamation affects the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument north-west of Hawaii — the largest of the three, spanning waters first protected by George W. Bush in 2006 and dramatically expanded by Barack Obama in 2016 — as well as the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument near Guam and Rose Atoll Marine National Monument near American Samoa. Both of the latter were established under Bush in 2009. Together the three cover nearly 500,000 square miles. Only U.S.-flagged vessels may fish commercially in the reopened zones; some restrictions within 50 nautical miles of certain Hawaiian islands and 12 nautical miles of Rose Atoll remain in place.

Speaking at the signing, Trump framed the closures as an economic wound. "With today's action we are officially reopening nearly half a million square miles of water around the northwestern Hawaiian islands," he said. "It ruined a big industry, by the way." Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick called it "restoring U.S. seafood competitiveness," arguing that fishing restrictions forced American fleets into international waters where they compete against less-regulated foreign operations.

## Science against the current

Conservation groups dispute that framing on both ecological and economic grounds. Earthjustice attorney David Henkin argued that "commercial fishing in our protected marine monuments would not only be disastrous for the environment, but also does nothing for the fishing industry" — noting that U.S. fleets already reach annual tuna catch limits without accessing monument waters. Oceana's Ben Enticknap put the scientific case more directly: the closed zones function as breeding and feeding grounds that replenish adjacent fisheries. Since Papahānaumokuākea's fishing ban was expanded in 2016, tuna abundance in surrounding waters has measurably increased, a trend researchers cite as the spillover effect that monument protections are designed to produce.

The monuments shelter ecosystems with no equivalent elsewhere — hydrothermal vents, ancient coral, endangered Hawaiian monk seals, and thousands of species found nowhere else on Earth. The Center for Biological Diversity called Thursday's action "a reckless attack on the world's greatest ocean sanctuaries."

Thursday's proclamation is the latest in a series: Trump reopened Atlantic protected fishing areas in February 2026 and targeted the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument in April 2025, only for a federal court to strike down that order in August 2025 on legal grounds. Whether Thursday's broader action will face a similar challenge — and whether that earlier ruling offers a template for litigation — is the question conservation attorneys are now working through. The courts, not the administration, may have the last word.

trump-clayton-dni-nomination.headline: Trump nominates SEC veteran Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence
trump-clayton-dni-nomination.body_md:
President Donald Trump has nominated Jay Clayton — the former chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission who currently serves as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York — to lead the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. The announcement, made Thursday, comes after a week of bipartisan uproar over Trump's earlier decision to install Bill Pulte, the director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, as acting intelligence chief.

Pulte had no intelligence or national security experience. More pointedly, he had used his FHFA position to dig up mortgage records against figures the White House regards as adversaries — including a Federal Reserve board member and a sitting senator. That conduct drove Democrats to a hardball tactic: blocking reauthorisation of Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, the legal basis for key signals-intelligence collection against foreign targets. The authority was set to lapse for the first time since its creation, and without Democratic votes, congressional leaders could not move a short-term extension. Clayton's nomination reads, in part, as a direct response to that standoff.

## A Financial Regulator Heads for Langley

Clayton's path to intelligence oversight is a circuitous one. He spent more than two decades at Sullivan & Cromwell, advising corporations on mergers, securities offerings, and regulatory proceedings — navigating deals including Barclays' acquisition of Lehman Brothers during the 2008 crisis. Trump tapped him to chair the SEC in 2017; he served until the end of 2020. After a brief return to private life, Trump brought him back in April 2025 as acting U.S. attorney in Manhattan, a position he has held on an indefinite basis since judges formalised the appointment that August.

His credentials are formidable in finance and law, modest in the traditional intelligence sense. The law that governs the DNI role calls for "extensive" national security experience. Clayton does not have it — at least not in the way the statute envisages. What he does have is credibility among lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. Senator Mark Warner said he had "great respect" for Clayton; Representative Jim Himes, the ranking Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, called his "intelligence, temperament and deep commitment to public service" fitting for the role. The Senate Intelligence Committee scheduled a confirmation hearing for June 17.

For market observers, the nomination's sharpest edge is what it reveals about personnel priorities in Trump's second term. Clayton's move to DNI vacates the SDNY's top post — a perch with direct implications for financial fraud and securities enforcement in New York. Separately, the SEC is itself in an unsettled moment: Paul Atkins, confirmed as chairman in April 2025 to complete Gary Gensler's term, technically reached the end of that term on June 5. Whether Trump renominates Atkins or reaches elsewhere is unresolved.

The FISA question is the more immediate clock. Even with Clayton's nomination on the table, Section 702 authority remains expired for now — its renewal still requires votes, and Democrats have indicated they want confirmation, not just a nomination, before they move. That vote is the first real test of how far Clayton's bipartisan goodwill extends.

rio-tinto-sandvik-autonomous-drilling.headline: Rio Tinto and Sandvik move toward autonomous surface drilling in new integration pact
rio-tinto-sandvik-autonomous-drilling.body_md:
Rio Tinto has operated autonomous drill rigs in Western Australia's Pilbara region since 2008. On June 1, it announced a collaboration with Swedish equipment maker Sandvik to extend that track record to a new hardware platform — Sandvik's i-series surface blasthole rigs — but the terms of the deal reveal little about when, or whether, any of this reaches full deployment.

> **In one sentence:** Rio Tinto and Sandvik are jointly developing autonomous surface drilling, but the announcement covers integration testing, not a fleet order.

The agreement pairs Sandvik's AutoMine® automation software with Rio Tinto's proprietary Autonomous Drilling System, known internally as ADS™. The stated objective is multi-rig, multi-site remote operation of Sandvik hardware managed through Rio Tinto's Perth Operations Centre — the same facility that already monitors haul trucks, production drills and autonomous trains from more than 1,500 kilometres away.

What the announcement does not include: a fleet purchase order, a disclosed investment figure, a deployment timeline, or a count of rigs involved. The first step is development and testing at Sandvik's test facility in Finland. Site-based trials at Rio Tinto's Western Australian operations follow, with performance assessed against specific production targets. That sequence describes early-stage integration work — the kind that typically precedes a commercial contract, not the contract itself.

## A fleet built over nearly two decades

Rio Tinto first trialled the ADS at its West Angelas mine in 2008 and expanded to 20 autonomous drills across two Pilbara sites by the end of 2018. By mid-2026, it operates 40 autonomous drills across seven mine sites. Its most technologically advanced operation, Gudai-Darri — opened in 2022 at a cost of $2.6 billion — runs three Caterpillar MD6310 autonomous production drills alongside 23 autonomous haul trucks, all monitored remotely from Perth.

![A surface drill rig operating in the Pilbara region of Western Australia, similar to the terrain where Rio Tinto's autonomous drilling field trials will take place](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4c/Drill_rig%2C_Pilbara%2C_August_2007.jpg)

The Sandvik pact is notable in part because Gudai-Darri's drilling automation was built around Caterpillar equipment. Connecting a different vendor's rigs to the ADS requires non-trivial integration — software bridging between Sandvik's Intelligent Control System Architecture and Rio Tinto's own control stack, hardware-level compatibility testing, and validation that multi-rig autonomous behaviour holds up in demanding Pilbara conditions. That is the work the Finland testing phase is meant to begin.

The case for it is clear enough. Autonomous drilling's productivity advantage has been well-documented in Rio Tinto's own estate: the company's Iron Ore Company of Canada trial of an autonomous electric blasthole drill in Labrador — its first deployment in a subarctic climate — recorded a 20 per cent improvement in average penetration rate compared to manually operated rigs during the first quarter of 2026. A single operator can monitor and control up to eight rigs from a centralised console, reducing the exposure of workers to blast zones and cutting the dead time that comes with shift changes.

Sandvik's president of surface drilling, Petri Virrankoski, framed the rationale in terms of interoperability: "This joint development reflects Sandvik's commitment to improving safety and productivity through open, interoperable automation. Building on AutoMine and our i-series platform, we are proud to extend our long-standing relationship with Rio Tinto and support the continued development of autonomous drilling for demanding Pilbara conditions."

No Rio Tinto executive statement accompanied the announcement — a notable omission for a deal being presented as a meaningful step forward. The absence of numbers, timelines and deployment specifics is consistent with a vendor collaboration in its early technical phase rather than an agreed-upon programme with committed capital. Whether the field trials produce a commercial result is the question this announcement leaves open.

The next indicator to watch for: performance results from Rio Tinto's Western Australian trial sites. If autonomous Sandvik rigs hit the production targets set for the field programme, a formal equipment order would be the logical follow-on. Until that announcement arrives, this remains a promising handshake.
